title: Ocean tides spin around spots where the sea barely rises or falls at all
body: On a planet with no continents, tides would be [vast bulges of water sweeping west](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4821/) with the Moon and Sun. On Earth, coastlines trap and reflect the tidal waves and the planet's spin turns them, so in each ocean basin the high water **rotates around a point** where the sea level hardly changes between high and low tide. These are called amphidromic points, and the farther a coast is from one, the bigger its tides tend to be. In the North Atlantic the tide circles anticlockwise, small in mid-ocean and large along the coasts of north-west Europe and Britain.

slides.prompt: The tide does something odd around New Zealand. What?
slides.answer: It can be high on one side and low on the other
slides.detail: The tidal wave is trapped and runs around the islands in about 12.5 hours, so the whole country acts like one giant amphidromic point.

slides.heading: Mapped by flying tide gauges
slides.text: The TOPEX/Poseidon and Jason satellites measured sea height from orbit for years. From those records, plus the motion of the Sun and Moon, scientists can predict the tide at any spot in the ocean at any time.

slides.heading: Why the tide goes round in circles

steps.label: The Moon and Sun raise bulges of water
Coastlines block and reflect the tidal wave
Earth's spin deflects the moving water
High water circles an amphidromic point

slides.question: What happens to the tide as you move away from an amphidromic point?
slides.explanation: At the point itself high and low tide are almost the same height. The range, the gap between them, increases with distance, though not evenly.
